title: Picture Book Lessons (Mary Kole, Good Story Company)
rule: Never say the lesson or theme aloud anywhere in the narrative. Show the character living through it and changing behaviour; put explanation in back matter for nonfiction. Kids are told what to do all day and do not want it from the book.
example: Not 'Gosh, kindness is so great' but a character acting kindly and others responding well; a climate story shows a character changing her own habits instead of telling readers not to use single-use plastic.
llm_tell: Stated morals and tidy takeaway lines, which Kole says she sees in many manuscripts, are the same morals-inserted tell the skill already lists for fiction.

title: Books That Teach Life Lessons (Kidlit.com, Mary Kole)
rule: Litmus test: remove the lesson from the end; if the story still stands alone it is not didactic, and if the plot exists only to deliver the moral, rebuild from character and conflict. A stated lesson makes agents and editors uncomfortable.
example: Cited failing ending: a girl closes with a line about letting her sisters pick the movie.
llm_tell: Plot built backwards from a moral, ending on a line that states it.

title: Picture Book Tips and Tricks (Writers Helping Writers)
topic: picture book craft: length, rhyme, art notes, read-aloud
rule: Under 500 words, nonfiction a bit more, cut filler like 'that' and 'just'. Rhyme must scan and must not flip word order for the rhyme ('Yoda talk'). Leave room for the illustrator: no stage directions, and avoid scenes with no visual variety such as two characters talking in a kitchen. Read it aloud; short snappy sentences with rhythm. The child protagonist solves the problem, not an adult. End on a twist or extra that invites rereading.
example: 'Make sure rhyming manuscripts scan correctly.' 'Let the illustrator decide how to fill in the rest of the details.'

title: Writing Picture Books (Institute for Writers; summary of Mem Fox and others)
topic: picture book craft: length, art notes, rhyme
rule: Word counts exclude art notes; editors dislike writers directing the illustrator and strip pointless notes; do not explain in text what the art will show (Mem Fox, secondhand). A claim that publishers have banned rhyme from unagented writers after many weak submissions comes from one advice site and is unverified.

title: Checklist: Preparing Your Manuscript for Critique (SCBWI Central California)
rule: The checklist includes the prompt 'beware of being didactic or preachy' and asks whether the story has a universal theme. Only a search snippet was read, not the page.

title: MDPI Informatics 12(4):139, AI-generated vs human-written children's stories with first and second graders and parents
topic: LLM children's stories: vocabulary and reader response
rule: Secondhand via a search summary, page returned 403: 30 first-graders, 81 second-graders and 103 parents often rated AI stories close to human ones. Human-authored stories tended to exceed young readers' vocabulary level, while AI stories kept vocabulary complexity controlled. Multimodal models and Chinese fairy tales, not ChatGPT. Treat as unverified until the paper is read.
llm_tell: Vocabulary held safely at level, i.e. no stretch words, where human stories reach above the child's own reading level. Unverified.

title: Tales of Morality: Comparing Human- and LLM-Generated Moral Stories from Visual Cues (Rezapour, Jeoung, You, Diesner, Findings of EMNLP 2025)
rule: Bibliographic record confirmed (pp. 18915-18933). The finding that human stories show a balanced spread of moral foundations and coherent arcs, while LLMs over-emphasise Care and often lack emotional resolution, comes from a search summary only; abstract pages returned 404 and the search could not confirm it. Not limited to children's stories. Unverified.
llm_tell: Care/kindness as the default moral, and arcs without emotional resolution. Unverified.

title: AI children's books, body horror edition (lcamtuf)
rule: Author collected about 220 AI children's books (count from a snippet) and says the point is that they are 'all the same'; the post is about illustrations and 'deliberately sidestepped the question of quality'. It says nothing about the text, so it is not evidence about prose tells. Closing line: 'You lose more than you might be expecting if you let an LLM be your voice.'
llm_tell: Sameness across a batch, not any one weak book (illustration-level evidence only).

title: Amazon's AI-generated children's books flood gift piles (AI Weekly, relaying Wired)
rule: Secondhand: researchers counted 517+ AI-generated nonfiction children's books on Amazon and Amazon removed 198 flagged titles. Spotted by cover errors, synthetic author profiles, copied series branding (Little People Big Dreams, Who Was?), and extreme reviews, i.e. by metadata and cover, not prose. One TechRadar writer names 'heartwarming' as a tell, unverified. Personalised gift books (child's name and photo) were sold by startups.
llm_tell: The detection signals reported are packaging and metadata. No published prose-level tell list for children's text was found.

title: Lessons Without Borders? Evaluating Cultural Alignment of LLMs Using Multilingual Story Moral Generation
rule: Snippet only: GPT-4o morals compared with human morals across languages; some human morals were flagged as highly similar to LLM output. Not read; details unknown.

title: Library and Lexile guides (cmlibrary.libguides.com, bookroo.com, arlibrary.libguides.com) via search summary
rule: Secondhand: Lexile measures text difficulty only, not theme, quality or age fit. Read-alouds usually run two to three grade levels above what the child can read alone, and picture books are often marked adult-directed with high Lexile numbers. So a high Lexile on a picture book is normal, and the rule is to write for the ear of a child listening, not for a reading-level formula. No search reached Beck/McKeown Tier 2 vocabulary work.
